extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and newspaper editors (wartime public)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and editing news dispatches about military operations during wartime, emphasizing attribution, operational detail, and contextual strategic explanation. Applies to wire-service/press reporting of battles, invasions, and related political/economic items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and agency attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin items with a clear dateline (location, province/state) and date, and show the news agency or service (e.g., 'WHITEHORSE, Y.T., FEB 17-(CANADIAN PRESS)=').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard wire-service dateline format so readers know where and when the report originated; include agency tag for sourcing and editorial chain-of-custody. Example on page: multiple datelines ('PEARL HARBOR, Feb. 18', 'WASHINGTON, Feb. 18').

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute assertions to named officials and ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: All interpretive or authoritative claims should be attributed to named sources with rank or office (e.g., 'said Brig. Gen. L.D. Worsham', 'Secretary of the Navy Knox said').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give full name and official title or rank to establish credibility and allow readers to weigh authority. When available, include location or affiliation of the speaker (Evansville, Ind., Pacific Fleet Headquarters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official communiqués verbatim and note their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote short official communiqués exactly (e.g., task forces had 'commenced' the assault) and explain what they do and do not reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproduce terse official language and immediately contextualize — highlight when communiqués are intentionally vague (often due to operational security) so readers understand the information ceiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report operational security constraints (radio silence) and their reporting impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain when and how radio silence or other security measures constrain reporting ('radio silence is imposed on ships... to prevent their location becoming known').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that lack of details can stem from security rules; avoid speculation and make explicit that some information cannot be disclosed because of operational security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulate and report conflicting sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When sources conflict (Tokyo radio reports vs. U.S. monitors), present both accounts and identify contradictions and source types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List each source, characterize its likely reliability (government communique, enemy broadcast, independent monitor), and make clear where accounts diverge rather than choosing one without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide geographic and strategic context
rubrics_metrics.description: Give distances, positions, and the strategic role of locations (e.g., Eniwetok is 'less than 400 statute miles northwest of Kwajalein' and 'has been used chiefly by the Nipponese as an operating base for their planes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include mileage, directional relationships, and why a location matters (airfield use, range to other bases) so readers understand operational significance and impact on broader campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify forces, units, and commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: List participating units and their commanders (e.g., '22nd Marines', '106th Army Infantry', 'Rear Admiral R.K. Turner'), and roles (amphibious forces, assault troops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide unit names/numbers and commanding officers to give concrete detail; specify service branch and command relationships when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report numeric specifics but indicate uncertainty where present
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide numbers (ship counts, tonnage, troop/regiment designations, costs like '$130,000,000') and, when precise totals are not confirmed, note that they are estimates or unconfirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise figures when sourced (photographs, official tallies) and mark estimates/unconfirmed figures explicitly to avoid misleading certainty (e.g., 'highest estimates set the total number...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Include relevant background and chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply historical context and project timelines (e.g., Canol project start date 'June 29, 1942', purpose, and terms of agreement) to situate current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly summarize prior events, origin dates, and policy/contractual conditions that bear on the present story so readers see continuity and cause-effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reconnaissance/photographic/evidence reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report findings from reconnaissance flights or photographic evidence explicitly (e.g., 'a reconnaissance flight... counted 25 enemy warships in Truk's lagoon').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the reconnaissance source and its findings; explain how that evidence supports claims (visibility, photograph confirmation), including limitations (cloud cover, rift in clouds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag unknowns and avoid unwarranted speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: When information is lacking ('There still was no further word from Admiral Nimitz' or 'no information that it had been completed'), make that clear and resist filling gaps with conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly what is not known and the reason if available (security, silence), and present plausible scenarios only as labeled speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotes for official interpretation and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Include verbatim quotes from officials to convey interpretation or emphasis (e.g., Knox: 'the attack was a victory', Nimitz: 'powerful naval task forces . . . commenced an attack').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place quotes in context and attribute them; quotes can convey tone and official judgment that raw facts do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat enemy broadcasts and propaganda cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: When using enemy radio or broadcasts (Tokyo radio), report content but frame it as possible propaganda or strategic messaging ('the broadcast...poo-poohed the importance' or gave an impression rather than confirmed fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate the broadcast's intended audience and potential bias; corroborate with independent monitors where possible and avoid taking enemy claims at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain operational implications and strategic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect tactical events to broader operational consequences (e.g., capturing Eniwetok would 'enable the United States to bomb Truk with land-based planes' and bring other bases within range).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate battlefield or base captures into their strategic effects (range, supply lines, staging airfields) so readers understand longer-term significance.
